name: Sandy Bell's
description: Sandy Bell's began as an ordinary Forrest Road grocery shop, and the pub's narrow, oddly proportioned interior still gives that away. It was already a bar by the 1920s, run by an owner named Mrs Bell, before regulars started calling it simply 'Sandy Bell's' - a nickname that stuck for over fifty years before it ever appeared on a sign. From the 1960s, under landlord Jimmy Cairney, it became one of the true engine rooms of the Scottish folk revival, hosting nightly sessions and after-hours 'kitchen ceilidhs' that drew players from across the city and abroad. Hamish Henderson, the poet and folklorist often called the father of that revival, held informal court here for years. It only adopted 'Sandy Bell's' as its official name in the early 1990s.
interesting_fact: Musicians who passed through its sessions include Barbara Dickson, Billy Connolly, Gerry Rafferty, Aly Bain, Johnny and Phil Cunningham, and Dick Gaughan - and the influential folk group Jock Tamson's Bairns formed out of chance meetings at the bar. Traditional Scottish and Irish sessions still run here most nights, making it one of the longest continuously running folk-music pubs in the country.

name: Bristo Port (Flodden Wall)
address: Forrest Road (between nos. 5 and 7), Edinburgh EH1 2QQ
description: A small marker and a line of dark cobbles (setts) set into the pavement here trace the course of Edinburgh's Flodden Wall, the town's defensive perimeter begun in fearful haste after the catastrophic Scottish defeat at the Battle of Flodden in 1513. This spot marks the site of the Bristo Port - also called the Greyfriars or Society Port - a fortified gateway built around 1515 where the wall crossed what became Bristo Street, controlling movement in and out of the walled burgh. The gate itself vanished long before Forrest Road was cut through the area in the 1860s to link George IV Bridge with the university quarter, so almost nothing survives above ground; the gap in the modern paving, between numbers 5 and 7, is essentially all that is left to see of it.
interesting_fact: Bristo Port was a comparatively late addition to the Flodden Wall circuit, added as the built-up area crept south toward Greyfriars decades after the original wall line was hurriedly laid out in 1513 - a reminder that the 'town wall' visitors picture as one single ring was actually extended and patched piecemeal over more than a century.

name: Teviot Row House
description: Opened on 19 October 1889, Teviot Row House is generally reckoned to be the oldest purpose-built students' union building in the world - earlier student societies had simply borrowed rooms elsewhere, but this was designed and built from scratch for the job. Architects Sydney Mitchell and Wilson gave it a Scots Baronial look, with pinnacled drum towers and crow-stepped gables echoing the royal palaces at Holyrood and Falkland, built in warm Hailes sandstone. It was extended westward in 1902-05 to add a dining hall and further bars, then again with a plainer rear block in 1962. The site has older roots too: it once held a townhouse belonging to Lord Ross, later a lying-in hospital that operated here between 1793 and 1842, before the union building replaced it.
interesting_fact: Its 1889 opening was marked with a torch-lit student procession through the city that evening. The building still runs six bars and a debating hall for the university's students today - and every August, during the Edinburgh Festival, it transforms into the Gilded Balloon Fringe complex, one of the biggest multi-venue comedy hubs in the city.
source_notes: Architect, opening date and 'oldest purpose-built union' claim, plus prior site use as a lying-in hospital, from Wikipedia. Google Places confirms address as 13 Bristo Place.

name: Reid Concert Hall
description: Funded by the bequest of General John Reid, a British Army officer, flautist and composer who endowed Edinburgh University's Chair of Music, Reid Concert Hall opened on 14 February 1859, designed in an Italianate neoclassical style by the Scottish architect David Cousin. Its intimate 218-seat auditorium sits beneath a richly coffered, tunnel-vaulted ceiling, with a 1978 organ built by the German firm Jurgen Ahrend against the east wall. For well over a century the building also housed a remarkable museum gallery of historic instruments, assembled by Professor John Donaldson and long considered the oldest purpose-built musical instrument museum in Europe.
interesting_fact: That instrument collection moved out in 2017, relocating to St Cecilia's Hall on the Cowgate to form a single 5,000-object collection - so the display cases here stand empty today, though the hall still hosts concerts, including an annual Reid Concert every 13 February marking General Reid's birthday and his gift to the university. During the Festival Fringe it becomes 'The Cowbarn', an Underbelly comedy venue.

Confirmed the 2017 relocation of the instrument collection to St Cecilia's Hall so the description doesn't misleadingly imply a visitable museum still operates in this building today. name: McEwan Lantern Pillar
description: Standing at the edge of Bristo Square opposite McEwan Hall's entrance, this tall tapering pillar of Portland stone was designed by Robert Rowand Anderson - the same architect responsible for McEwan Hall itself - and erected around 1890. It combines a decorative lamp standard with carved detailing, including the McEwan family coat of arms, and was presented to the City of Edinburgh by the brewer and Liberal MP William McEwan alongside his much larger gift of the Hall, which opened a few streets away on 3 December 1897. McEwan had left school at fourteen to work in his uncle's brewery and built it into one of Scotland's largest, later ploughing a fortune into university buildings across the campus that still bear his name.
interesting_fact: Despite being a Category B listed structure in its own right, the lantern pillar is easy to walk straight past - most visitors' eyes go straight to the huge domed hall behind it, leaving this smaller companion piece from the same 1890s gift almost unnoticed on the square. It is officially catalogued by Historic Environment Scotland as the 'Corporation Lamp', a nod to the fact that it was a civic gift rather than purely a university one.

name: The Next Big Thing is a Series of Little Things
address: Bristo Square, Edinburgh (paving between the Dugald Stewart Building and McEwan Hall)
description: Easy to miss underfoot, this artwork by artist Susan Collis consists of around 1,600 small bronze dots set into the paving of Bristo Square, meandering roughly 68 metres from near the Dugald Stewart Building across to the entrance of McEwan Hall. Titled 'The Next Big Thing is a Series of Little Things', the piece resembles a trail of dripped paint spilled carelessly across the stone - a playful, almost invisible companion to the grand Victorian architecture surrounding the square, installed as part of a wider redevelopment of the square that also brought in new paving, seating and lighting for the university's central plaza.
interesting_fact: Collis designed the dots to change with use rather than stay fixed: as thousands of students' feet cross the square every day, the bronze studs slowly polish up brighter than the stone around them, so the artwork is quite literally still being finished by the people walking over it, years after it was installed. Its title plays on the cliche 'the next big thing', suggesting that grand ambitions are really just an accumulation of small, easily overlooked details - much like the dots themselves.
